body:
Amazing work! Thanks for putting the time in. In terms of getting an initial version merged I think these are some good goals. I think this should help get the general architecture defined and answer some of the open questions. I think your other TODOs can be added in subsequent PRs which will make things easier to review:
- Demo with full resolution support and window resizing.
- Lambert support only.
- Support for megakernal & wavefront path tracing to compare performance.
- Organize the files

In terms of making this easier to understand - do you mind splitting some of the code out into separate files? The "PathTracerCore" file is pretty monolithic and difficult to follow at the moment. I think these changes will make it easier to give some feedback:
- I think we can move the compute nodes to a `webgpu/nodes` folder.
- Lets remove commented code that's not being used
- Can we document a bit more of what's happening especially in the wavefront path tracer step?

And some other comments:
> So that leaves us with max tile resolution of 1920x1080

It would be helpful to know what data is needed at each step of the path tracer. But organizing things from the beginning so that tiled rendering is supported I think is our best bet. Once three.js supports requesting larger buffers users can use that but we'll still need a graceful fallback either way.

> At what point do you propose measuring performance?

Let's get to a point where we have a full resolution scene rendering and we can take a look at the pros / cons of the megakernal and wavefront approach. The wavefront approach may also wind up having more of a noticeable improvement later on when we can terminate rays early and / or sort them and therefore avoid running large blocks of work.

Also just a note that the "megakernel" path seems to not be working for me. I see this error:

```
'TRI_INTERSECT_EPSILON'
    if ( abs( det ) < TRI_INTERSECT_EPSILON ) {
                      ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^


 - While calling [Device].CreateShaderModule([ShaderModuleDescriptor ""compute""]).
```

@gkjohnson An update is overdue here. The initial implementation has poor performance on my computer. I'm seeing ~4ms (megakernel) -> ~8ms (wavefront) per frame with the same number of bounces. Going through the papers again I picked up a couple of differences that could be implemented here (see some of the PERFORMANCE todos). I tried implementing a couple of optimisations (atomic per workgroup, SoA structure) but they did not give meaningful improvement. Will try to experiment with queues and kernel configurations to lower memory bandwidth used.

Another finding from reading: wavefront pathtracers' performance should not degrade that much from more complicated materials. On the other hand, with megakernel complex materials will increase register usage per one thread hence limit possible parallelism. Therefore, I think it will be better to assess performance once pbr material is implemented.

Thanks for the update! I don't think we'll really wind up seeing the performance benefits until we have some kind of a full, ongoing ray-queue in place. I've been caught up in a number of other stuff recently but this is still on my list to take a deeper look at. Hopefully I'll be able to get to it in the next month or so 🙏

Yes, that was a WIP commit so did not even work 😅. It was for syncing between two of my machines.

Just pushed new commits with physical materials both in megakernel and wavefront pathtracers. No support for textures yet. 

Since then I was investigating performance profiles (with PIX) to try to figure out why pathtracers behave the way they do. But yes, it looks like we will need a different kernel setup with a consistent path state buffer and communication in queues through indices into the buffer rather than pure values. 

I will take a deeper look at #713 later today. How would like to proceed with the feature? Should this PR be closed in favor of #713 ? Is help on this still welcome?

> How would like to proceed with the feature? Should this PR be closed in favor of https://github.com/gkjohnson/three-gpu-pathtracer/pull/713 ? Is help on this still welcome?

Of course help is welcome! Your work here has been incredibly helpful and #713 is based on this branch - but I've moved things around in the process of understanding everything and trying to address some of the tiling questions.

Hopefully I'll have a first working pass at a wavefront tracer using a cyclic buffer in the next few days and we can see how the timing works out. But even so there are a lot of things that can happen in parallel. Working on the PBR materials as you've been doing here, for example, is fairly separable. Some of the other things that are becoming clear as I learn more about WebGPU compute:

- Interleaving and packing geometry buffer attributes into a single buffer rather than a bunch of separate storage buffers would help reduce the number of necessary storage buffers, which there's apparently a limit for. It would also make it easier to fetch the full set of vertex data. I'm not sure how a larger struct would impact the BVH traversal, though.
- Exploring using the new three-mesh-bvh [ObjectBVH](https://github.com/gkjohnson/three-mesh-bvh/blob/master/example/src/bvh/ObjectBVH.js) for storing a top-level acceleration structure for things like the scene and instanced / batched mesh geometries would be big improvement and make it easier to initialize and render the scene.
- In terms of path tracing architecture - bidirectional path tracing is something I'd like to incorporate, but it's something I'm less familiar with if you have any knowledge or interest here.
- Background transparency is something I'd like to get figured out.

Regarding the PRs - I'm happy to merge the other PR into this one or we can start making PRs into the webgpu-pathtracer branch. Either one is good to me to treat as a the "webgpu dev" branch once a basic wavefront implementation is one.

> Interleaving and packing geometry buffer attributes into a single buffer rather than a bunch of separate storage buffers

I've been thinking of packing only color + uv + normals into one attributes buffer. (maybe material index?) And leave position in a separate buffer to not hinder ray tracing performance. That also allows for more vertices to be used in a geometry. There is a default limit of 128Mb for a buffer size. So that's <2.8mil vertices if packing every attribute into one buffer.

> Hopefully I'll have a first working pass at a wavefront tracer using a cyclic buffer in the next few days and we can see how the timing works out.

I am curious to try my hand at different architectures to try and optimize the pathtracer. I would like to try to make an architecture in parallel and then compare performance, if that's okay with you. 

With a consistent ray queue 'execution time' becomes a less relevant metric because a megakernel 'sample' and a wavefront 'sample' cast different amount of rays. Ray count seems to be a good metric only in closed scene because there could be rays that go directly to the environment evaluation like in webgpu_primitives. So perhaps a different scene is needed to properly assess performance characteristics.

webgpu-pathtracer branch seems a lot more structured so I will change this PR's target branch and resolve conflicts, hopefully soon.

> I've been thinking of packing only color + uv + normals into one attributes buffer. (maybe material index?)

Packing the non-BVH buffers is probably a good place to start. Once a TLAS / full scene definition is used we should be able to get rid of the per-vertex material index, as well.

> I am curious to try my hand at different architectures to try and optimize the pathtracer. I would like to try to make an architecture in parallel and then compare performance, if that's okay with you.

That sounds great - it will be good to compare notes. With the changes in #713 the "WebGPUPathTracer" has been structured to be able use different "backends" (eg "WaveFrontPathTracer" & "MegaKernalPathTracer") it should be easy to work on multiple of these backends in parallel and compare performance. Having a "PathTracerBackend" superclass may be a good model to move to. Alternatives like an "AOMapBackend" or "LightMapBackend" could fit into this architecture nicely in the future, as well.

> Ray count seems to be a good metric only in closed scene because there could be rays that go directly to the environment evaluation like in webgpu_primitives. So perhaps a different scene is needed to properly assess performance characteristics.

Agreed on different scenes but I think it's going to be difficult to have just one to rely on. At least one enclosed and one open (like we have) would be good - having rays that terminate immediately because they go to the skybox directly is one of the big merits of the wavefront approach, I think: we shouldn't be spending time on rays that don't need it. Being able to skip initialization of rays once they reach their target sample count or are detected to converge are some of the optimizations that will really make the benefits apparent.

@gkjohnson - I've changed this to be a PR into webgpu-pathtracer branch. Now this changes:
- Add a second wavefront implementation with storage textures. A quick profile did not reveal any effect on performance from using storage textures compared with storage buffers.
- Add ability to choose between three different "backends": MegaKernel, WaveFront and PathTracerCore (added in this PR)
- Add basic support for pbr materials in all pathtracing "backends"
- Use two different target storage textures: one to read from and another to write to. It turns out, <rgba32float, read_write> storage textures are not supported by default and need to be requested from the webgpu. For now only in megakernel because that involves copying a texture and in wavefront pathtracers that would need to be done after each step. I think we should enable two different textures and copy them only on devices that do not support read_write f32 texture. How critical do you think this is?

WaveFrontPathTracer's image appear to become unchanged after a quick while. That looks very much like pRNG being predictable or same after some point. However I could not find a bug. Maybe its more clear to you?

Material samples with pdf <= 0 tripped me up on a number of occasions. Why would code sample directions that are basically impossible? There is a specific glsl if statement that filters them out, so that's expected? It seems like a waste of resources to calculate a ray that's impossible. What am I missing?

--

PathTracerCore approach

For each pixel in a tile there is an entry in pathState array that contains the entirety of the state needed for that path. However pixels from different tiles can be traced at the same time.

1. Process all pixels and see if path is terminated: maximum bounce count reached, there was no hit on last step or throughput is set to 0. For terminated paths accumulate color and add to queue for "regeneration". For non-terminated - add to queue for material evaluation of the last hit. Queues for communication contain only indices for target paths.
2. For every path in a queue for regeneration write a new ray to trace and reset other components: throughput, pcgState and tileOffset of the "current tile". That offset is used to determine global position of the pixel in the image when accumulating color. Indices of regenerated paths are placed onto extension ray queue.
3. Material evaluation. Take data about latest hit from the pathState, calculate material response and place results back into pathState. If an extension ray is generated, index is placed onto extension ray queue.
4. Intersect rays from extension ray queue against scene and place results into pathState. Go to step 1 to process results.

This is slightly modified same flow as in [Megakernels considered harmful](https://research.nvidia.com/sites/default/files/pubs/2013-07_Megakernels-Considered-Harmful/laine2013hpg_paper.pdf) paper. Originally, extension ray queue contained rays - not indices - and there is and a queue to place intersection results into.

--

In my testing PathTracerCore performs worse than WaveFrontPathTracer on 5 waves: 2.2ms vs 1.4ms

In general, I like WaveFrontPathTracer approach more for communication in queues with values. The fact that that pixels are not hardcoded gives us an ability to better handle different "complexity" pixels as you mentioned in https://github.com/gkjohnson/three-gpu-pathtracer/pull/713#issuecomment-3863520265

Overall, memory bandwidth seems to really be a bottleneck. Next on the optimisation list:
- WaveFrontPathTracer suffers from low utilization when appending paths to the queue. Empty indirectDispatches seem to seep time. It seems that queue can only handle 1-2 tiles at a time. Maybe we can cycle through tiles, not trying to add all of them all the time?
- Reads from pathState in all but logic kernels are random, because queues are just indices. Original paper lays data out in SoA fashion for better cache-line utilization and less actual fetches. 
- I wonder if "compressing" path state is a worthwhile investment. I've seen a paper about packing wide bvh and using every bit to decrease the amount of fetches or increase the amount of nodes fetch in one fetch.
- A balance between passing indices/values in queues. There are values that are read/written at different locations without any modifications e.g. pixel, throughput, currentBounce etc. Which could probably be passed by an index into pathState, rather than by value, decreasing read/write amount directly to the queues at the cost of scattering values across the memory when accessed.

--

>  we can reduce the amount of rays processed per frame based on framerate and the page can remain responsive since the whole 7+ bounce path doesn't need to finish in a single pass

Agreed, this decoupling is great. 

> Add support for a maximum sample count to prevent adding and working on rays for pixels that will have "finished" more quickly.

I really liked your idea to store active flag in sample count texture. We could store more meta information in those two textures: two-three channels in sample count texture and theoretically an alpha channel in output target. Variance could be stored similarly, for example.

Curious to hear what you think.

Thanks! There's a lot here so I'm going to focus on the path tracing logic - I think it would be best to keep things like PBR materials to a separate PR so it's easier to follow and discussed what's changed. But thanks for putting this together - One of the issues that sticks out to me is that even though a subsequent tile is adding rays to the queue it's possible, if not likely, that pixels will be passed over because paths from the previous tile are taking up the available path state slots. Setting the number of iterations to "1" is an extreme example but demonstrates it in this simple scene. In a more complex scene with more bounces you can imagine this happening much more frequently resulting in less even sample distribution across the image:
These are separable issues, though, and I think there may be some value to being able to keeping path state in a single buffer while modeling the other buffers as uints but it's hard to say what may be a benefit or not with large sets of changes. Ultimately I think the two approaches we've taken are pretty well-aligned and there's likely a solution in the middle that will be a good place to land an initial version of the path tracer logic. It might be best to make smaller more targeted changes so we can discuss the merit of these things and test the performance in a more targeted way (eg switch to a logic kernel, switch to a path state buffer, etc). To some of the other comments: > I think we should enable two different textures and copy them only on devices that do not support read_write f32 texture. How critical do you think this is? To start I think we should just use the same code path for every device and we can use a "ping pong" approach for blending the sample textures. It might be more optimal to check the capabilities and use a single texture if possible but every option like this is another level of complexity and something that needs to be tested so I think it will be easiest to support just one code path for the moment. > Material samples with pdf <= 0 tripped me up on a number of occasions. Why would code sample directions that are basically impossible? There are two separate normals per triangle - the "geometric" normals which represent the actual geometry used for raycasting against and "shading" normals which represent the interpolated normals used to imply a rounded surface. When these normals don't align a ray can effectively be coming from "underneath" the shading normal hemisphere resulting in an invalid PDF. The PBR Book mentions it [in section 9.1](https://pbr-book.org/3ed-2018/Materials/BSDFs). There are probably better solutions for this but they haven't been implemented here, yet. > WaveFrontPathTracer's image appear to become unchanged after a quick while. That looks very much like pRNG being predictable or same after some point. However I could not find a bug. Maybe its more clear to you? It's working in the other branch so it must be related to changes made in this one. I'm not sure if it's related but I see that the "QueuedHit" struct was modified to add a "side" field without adjusting the structure size. > WaveFrontPathTracer suffers from low utilization when appending paths to the queue. Empty indirectDispatches seem to seep time. It seems that queue can only handle 1-2 tiles at a time. Maybe we can cycle through tiles, not trying to add all of them all the time? One of the reasons I marched through all tiles is was to prepare, at least notionally, for skipping pixels that have already been "finished". Once this is the case the marching through only 1 or 2 tiles may only yield a few new rays added to the queue, which would be a different issue. Is it actually the case that dispatching an empty compute call is a time sink? Or is it an artifact of how the timing is being measured? I would this this would be fairly cheap, though I agree that Ideally we would be able to skip it entirely.
Closed in favor of #713 with different features migrating from here in multiple smaller PRs
